title: Jerusalem's Leaders on Trial
summary: The Lord announces that he will take away everything Jerusalem relies on: food, water, soldiers, judges, prophets, and counselors, leaving the city to inexperienced rulers and social chaos. He takes the elders and leaders to court for devouring his vineyard and grinding the faces of the poor. Then he turns to the proud women of Jerusalem, whose finery will be replaced with rope, baldness, and sackcloth as the city mourns its fallen men.
story: Chapter 2 ended with the warning to stop trusting in man. Chapter 3 shows what happens when God removes the human supports people trust. It continues the section that began in 2:1 and moves from the general day of the Lord to its concrete effects on Jerusalem's society. The leaders who should have protected the weak have exploited them, and the city's wealth, displayed in the clothing and jewelry of its women, has been built on that exploitation. The chapter is bleak, but a few lines keep hope open: verse 10 promises that the righteous will enjoy the fruit of their labor, and chapter 4 will turn from ruin to a cleansed Zion.
historical:
The chapter describes Judah's ruling class in the eighth century BC: the mighty man and warrior, the judge and prophet, the elder and the commander of fifty. The commander of fifty was a military rank going back to Israel's early organization (Exodus 18:21; 2 Kings 1:9). Soothsayers, magicians, and enchanters, forbidden in Israel's law (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), are listed among those Jerusalem leaned on, a sign of how far official religion had drifted.

The promise of lads and children as rulers (verse 4) may describe a general collapse of competent leadership after war and deportation took away the experienced men, as happened when Babylon later removed Judah's leaders (2 Kings 24:14-16). Some scholars see a pointed reference to a particular young king, and Ahaz came to the throne young (2 Kings 16:2), but the text does not name anyone. The collapse Isaiah describes came in stages: the Assyrian devastation of Judah in 701 BC and, more fully, the Babylonian conquest of 587 or 586 BC.
cultural:
In a society without a state welfare system, elders and heads of households held communities together, judged disputes at the city gate, and cared for the vulnerable. A cloak (verse 6) was a basic possession, and in a devastated city having one was enough to qualify a man for leadership, though he refuses it. Israel pictured itself as God's vineyard (see chapter 5), so to devour the vineyard (verse 14) was to consume the very people the leaders were meant to tend.

The list of ornaments in verses 18 to 23 is the longest list of women's clothing and jewelry in the Bible. Several of its Hebrew words occur nowhere else, so some translations are informed guesses, but archaeologists have recovered many such items from the region: crescent-shaped pendants, anklets, nose rings, signet rings, perfume flasks, and small amulets. Some of these ornaments had religious or protective meaning as charms. Mirrors in this period were polished bronze. The reversal in verse 24 of fragrance, belt, styled hair, fine clothing, and beauty into stench, rope, baldness, sackcloth, and shame describes captives being led away, since conquerors stripped, bound, and sometimes shaved prisoners.
literary: The chapter falls into three parts. Verses 1 to 12 describe the collapse of social order, with lists of the officials God will remove and short dramatic speeches (verses 6-7) of men refusing to lead. Verses 13 to 15 are a courtroom scene: the Lord rises to contend and brings his charge directly against the elders and leaders. Verses 16 to 26 turn to the daughters of Zion, whose pride is described in vivid detail and then undone by a series of instead of reversals. The chapter ends with the city itself personified as a woman sitting on the ground in mourning. Verses 10 and 11, set as a small wisdom saying about the righteous and the wicked, interrupt the gloom to state the moral order beneath the judgment.

outline.t: Why Jerusalem stumbles, and the righteous and the wicked
The Lord's case against the elders and leaders
The pride of the daughters of Zion undone
The city mourns its fallen men

doctrines.note: God's judgment here works largely by removing what people rely on and letting the consequences of injustice unfold. The collapse of leadership is itself a judgment.
The chapter shows sin as social as well as personal. Leaders who plunder the poor and a wealthy class displaying its luxury are condemned together, and pride is named as the root in both.
The Lord is the one who removes supply and support and who rises to judge. The chaos of verses 4 to 7 does not escape his rule; it is part of it.

words.note: Riv, to contend or bring a case. It is the verb of a lawsuit, and in verse 13 the Lord rises as prosecutor. The prophets often use this word for God's case against his people, and it frames the leaders' crimes as breaches of covenant, not only bad policy.

Mish'an, support or staff, something to lean on. In verse 1 it appears in paired forms, translated supply and support. The point is that everything Jerusalem leans on, from bread to military men, can be taken away, leaving only God to trust.

Ani, poor or afflicted. The word describes people who are powerless and exposed to abuse. In verses 14 and 15 the leaders have plundered them and ground their faces, and God calls them My people, siding with them against their rulers.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is mainly by contrast. It describes shepherds who devour the flock, and the Bible's answer to failed leaders is a true shepherd and king. Ezekiel 34 develops this at length, and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), in contrast to those who exploit them. The reversal of pride and humiliation in verses 16 to 24 anticipates Mary's song, where God brings down rulers from their thrones and lifts up the humble (Luke 1:52), and Jesus' warnings against those who devour widows' houses (Mark 12:40). The New Testament also warns against trusting adornment rather than character (1 Peter 3:3-4). The hope that the righteous will enjoy the fruit of their deeds points forward to the one righteous king Isaiah will soon introduce.

hard.q: Is it fair that the women of Jerusalem are singled out and that women ruling is described as a judgment?
hard.a: Readers today notice that verse 12 lists women ruling alongside youths as a sign of disorder, and that verses 16 to 24 single out women's finery. Several points help. The passage reflects the social order of Isaiah's day, in which rule by the young and by women was unusual, and its point is that the normal structures of society have collapsed, not a general statement about women's capacities. The Greek translation and some modern scholars read the Hebrew word in verse 12 with different vowels as creditors or extortioners rather than women, which would change the line considerably; the Hebrew text as vocalized reads women. The indictment of the daughters of Zion is not about women as such but about the wealthy class of Jerusalem, whose luxury was bought with the plunder of the poor (verses 14-15); the men of that class have just been indicted. Both are judged for the same sin, and the whole city, men and women, suffers the consequences together (verses 25-26).

questions: What supports in your life would you be most afraid to lose, and what would it mean to trust God if they were removed?
The leaders are charged with grinding the faces of the poor. Where might ordinary comfort be built on someone else's hardship?
Verses 10 and 11 insist that the righteous and the wicked will reap what they sow. How does that promise help when justice seems slow?
